The river behind you reached the coast. In the last chapter, the Upper Vell dam went; Tomas Lind’s chalet stayed standing. He asks me not to tell him which kettles; he would like to imagine all of them. Earlier, the field cabin above the third falls was lost. Its shelf of notebooks had already been emptied when Tomas gave them to me. I am Mara Vey. I kept those pages because numbers, unlike councils, can be made to sit still in a box.

Gil Harrow wrote that Riverside deferred the spillway in 2009 and 2016. The national inspectors called the dam satisfactory; the harbour needed dredging, the school roof leaked, and he believed there was time. In 2017, households voted down the yearly levy. One spoilt paper said, “I would if I could.” The wall came later, built to the old design. No single hand made the river, but some signatures carried farther than others.

Tomas’s letter asks for a new stake line, higher up, where ice remains. Not to change this year. To know where you are. I have left the letter open beside my pencil, and the higher stake line still waits to be drilled.
